title: Wing flaps
object: Electrically driven single-slotted flaps of a four-seat high-wing light aircraft: the wing cut through the inboard flap track, the 28 V jackscrew actuator in section, the bellcranks, push-pull rods and crossed cables in plan, and the cockpit selector with its follow-up switches
idea: A curved track turns one push into two motions: first the flap slides aft and the wing grows, then it turns down and opens a slot that keeps the air on the flap
summary: Each flap rides on two rollers in one curved slot. While both rollers are on the slot's straight part the flap only slides aft (Fowler motion: the chord grows up to 5 %); when the slot curves, the aft roller drops ahead of the forward one and the flap turns down, opening a gap of 2 % of the chord between its nose and the shroud. Air from under the wing jets through that gap over the flap, starting a fresh boundary layer that stays attached at 30°, so the lift curve moves up (C_L,max 1.46 to 1.78) and the wing stalls at a lower angle and a lower speed (53 to 48 kt). A 28 V motor turns a self-locking Tr16×4 jackscrew through 25:1 spur gears; the nut swings a bellcrank whose rod drives the starboard flap and whose crossed cables drive the port bellcrank. A follow-up cable turns the selector's switch carrier, so the motor stops when the flaps reach the selected angle; limit switches stop it at 0° and 30°; full travel takes 9 s.
usedFor: Pilot training: what each flap setting does to lift, drag, attitude and stall speed, why the flaps take 9 seconds, why there is a flap limit speed
Aeronautical courses: Fowler and slotted flaps, the slot effect on the boundary layer, C_L against α, the stall speed from C_L,max
Machine design: a two-roller track as a cam, a self-locking jackscrew, a mechanical follow-up servo and limit switches, a crossed-cable interconnect
